transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been troubling you or what brings you here today?

Well… I came in because I just can’t seem to get anything in order anymore. It’s embarrassing to say, because it sounds like such a simple thing, but my kitchen table has turned into this whole pile of everything—my husband’s appointment papers, church flyers, notes from the senior center, little half-finished lists I start and then don’t finish. And I’ll sit there looking at all of it, thinking, “All right, I need to do something,” but I can’t seem to figure out which thing comes first.

Then before I know it, I’ve spent the whole day sort of shuffling papers around or staring at them, and nothing really gets done. It feels like my whole day disappears right there at the table. That’s really what brought me in.
When you sit at the table looking at all those papers, do you feel overwhelmed by them, like you don’t even know where to start, or is it more that you just don’t feel like doing anything at all?

It’s much more that I feel overwhelmed, I think. Not that I don’t care or that I’m just being lazy—because I do want to take care of it. I’ll sit down at the kitchen table and there’s just… papers everywhere. My husband’s appointment papers in one little stack, or what was supposed to be a stack, then church flyers, things from the senior center, little notes I wrote to myself, lists that I started and then got distracted from or didn’t finish.

And I look at it and I think, “Okay, I need to sort this out,” but then I can’t tell what should come first. Should I call about his appointment? Should I put the church thing on the calendar? Should I throw out the old papers? Should I make a new list from the other lists? And by the time I’m trying to decide, I feel like my mind just sort of jams up. I’ll move one paper over here and another paper over there, and then I’m right back where I started.

So no, it’s not that I don’t feel like doing anything. It’s that I can’t seem to get it in order enough to begin, and then somehow the whole day is gone.

Do you ever feel like you have intrusive or unwanted thoughts that cause you distress, or do you feel the need to do certain things over and over again to make yourself feel better or to prevent something bad from happening?

I’m not sure I have that, at least not in the way you’re describing it. I mean, I do get bothered by things when I’m sitting there looking at the mess, and I can feel very uneasy because I know something might be important and I don’t want to miss it. But I wouldn’t say I have a thought that keeps barging in over and over, like something terrible is going to happen unless I do some particular ritual.

And I don’t think I do things over and over to prevent something bad, no. I might pick up the same paper more than once, or reread the same note because I’ve lost track of what I was doing, but it’s not like I’m doing it to make a fear go away. It’s more that I can’t seem to hold the next step in my head clearly enough.

So… no, I don’t think so. Unless I’m misunderstanding what you mean.
Over the past few weeks, have you noticed feeling down, sad, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy?

I don’t know that I’d call it sad, exactly. I mean, I get discouraged, certainly, because I look around and think, “Why can’t I just handle these ordinary things?” And that can make me feel low for a bit.

But I haven’t really noticed losing interest in things in the way you might mean. If something pleasant is happening, I can still enjoy it. It’s more that I get bogged down and then I’m frustrated with myself afterward. I’m not sure if that counts as feeling down or if it’s just feeling worn out by the mess of it all.
Have you been feeling tired or having low energy a lot of the time, even when you haven’t been doing much?

I’m not sure I’d say low energy exactly. I mean, I do get tired, but I’ve been thinking of it more as sort of mentally worn out, if that makes sense. Like I can sit there not doing very much physically at all, just looking at things I need to deal with, and afterward I feel drained in my head.

But I don’t know that I wake up every day feeling exhausted for no reason, or that my body feels heavy all the time. It’s more that if I’ve been trying to sort through decisions or keep track of things, I feel used up, even though from the outside it probably looks like I haven’t done much. So… I haven’t really noticed a constant low energy, no. It’s more tied to getting overwhelmed, I think.
Do you find it very hard to get started on tasks, even simple ones, to the point that it’s affecting your daily life?

Yes, very much. That’s really why I came in, honestly. It isn’t just that I put something off because I don’t feel like doing it. I’ll sit down at the kitchen table meaning to handle one simple thing, like look at one of my husband’s appointment papers or put a church flyer where it belongs, and then I see the senior-center note, and the half-finished grocery list, and another little list I started, and I just… stop.

The whole table is covered with things that probably aren’t even all that complicated by themselves, but when they’re all sitting there together I can’t seem to decide what comes first. I’ll pick something up, then think, “No, maybe this is more urgent,” and then I’ll put it down and look at something else. And before I know it, I’ve spent half the day there and nothing is actually done.

It’s embarrassing because these are ordinary daily things, not big projects. But getting started feels like I have to untangle everything first, and I can’t get it into any order in my head. So yes, it’s affecting my life. The day just disappears while I’m trying to figure out where to begin.

As you were growing up, did you often have trouble focusing, staying organized, or sitting still? And do you still experience any of those kinds of difficulties today, even beyond what’s been happening at the kitchen table?

Yes… I think so. I didn’t really think of it that way at the time, of course, because when you’re a child you just think you’re being scolded, or you’re “not trying hard enough.” But I remember even when I was a little girl, my teachers would write things like I was bright, but careless. That word came up a lot, careless.

They’d say I forgot my books, or forgot to bring homework back, or that I needed reminders to finish my seatwork before I could go outside with the other children. And I did want to finish it—I wasn’t trying to be difficult. I’d start, and then somehow I’d drift or lose my place, and suddenly everyone else was lining up or going out and I still had things half-done.

So yes, looking back, it does feel like this isn’t brand-new. The kitchen table is just the current version of it, I suppose.

latest_inference.note: The patient's lifelong history of difficulty focusing, staying organized, and completing tasks, dating back to childhood, supports a diagnosis of ADHD (F90.0). The presentation is primarily inattentive type, with significant difficulties in initiating and organizing tasks, feeling overwhelmed by clutter, and mental fatigue related to decision-making, rather than classic depressive symptoms or OCD. The absence of persistent low mood, anhedonia, or ritualistic behaviors rules out F33.1 and F32.9. This turn ruled out other candidates and narrowed the diagnosis to F90.0.
